fields.why:
In BICAR-ICU (2018) bicarbonate gave no overall benefit; the
pre-specified subgroup with pH ≤ 7.2 plus AKI stage 2–3 showed a
signal of lower mortality and less dialysis. That subgroup
became the SSC 2021 suggestion. BICARICU-2 (JAMA 2025, n = 627,
pH ≤ 7.20 + AKI 2–3) then tested it directly: 90-day mortality
62.1% vs 61.7% (no benefit); only less kidney replacement
therapy (35% vs 50%). Bicarbonate also
makes CO2 (needs ventilation), lowers ionised calcium
and can worsen intracellular acidosis.

HY1|ABE-09.src: Jaber S et al. BICARICU-2 RCT. JAMA 2025;334(22):2000-2010. doi:10.1001/jama.2025.20231

fields.a:
- **HbA1c < 7%** (Newbie): **140-180** mg/dL
- **HbA1c > 7%** (Seasoned veteran), surgical: **140-180** mg/dL
- **HbA1c > 7%** (Seasoned veteran), medical: **180-220** mg/dL
- **Caution:** these HbA1c tiers are expert opinion, not guideline. **SCCM 2024**: start insulin at persistent BG **≥180 mg/dL**, keep the conventional **~140–180 mg/dL**, and avoid an intensive 80–139 target. **CONTROLING (2021, n = 2,075)**: an HbA1c-individualised target gave no benefit (90-day mortality ~32.8% vs 30.4%) and was stopped early.
MNEMONIC: **Newbies + Seasoned in SICU -> tight control. Seasoned in MICU -> relaxed window.**

CCM01|GLU-26.src: Honarmand K et al. SCCM glycemic control guideline 2024. Crit Care Med 2024;52(4):e161-e181; Bohe J et al. CONTROLING. Intensive Care Med 2021 (doi:10.1007/s00134-021-06526-8)

fields.a:
**Enteral within 24–48 h · hypocaloric week 1 · protein 1.2–2.0 (ASPEN) / 1.3 (ESPEN) g/kg**

a **Within 24–48 h** once haemodynamically stable — low or stable vasopressor doses are not a contraindication.
b Energy in week 1: **12–25 kcal/kg/day** (ASPEN 2022), full target ~25 kcal/kg later. Protein **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day** (ASPEN) or **1.3 g/kg/day reached progressively** (ESPEN 2023). Avoid early high protein: EFFORT Protein (≥2.2 g/kg) no benefit, possible harm with AKI or high SOFA; PRECISe (2.0 vs 1.3) worse functional recovery.
c **Hypocaloric** early (≤ 70% of target), reaching 80–100% after day 3.
d Only if enteral feeding falls short by **day 4–7** (ESPEN 3–7; ASPEN 7).

HY6|GIN-01.src: Compher JPEN 2022 (ASPEN/SCCM); Singer Clin Nutr 2023 (ESPEN); Heyland Lancet 2023;401:568 (EFFORT Protein); Bels Lancet 2024 (PRECISe)

fields.q:
Managing acute liver failure in the ICU:
a NAC: in whom does it work?
b Cerebral oedema — sodium target
c Ammonia above 150 with grade III–IV
d FFP for a high INR?
fields.a:
**NAC (proven in paracetamol; early-grade non-paracetamol) · Na 145–155 · CRRT for ammonia**

a **N-acetylcysteine**: proven in paracetamol ALF. In adult non-paracetamol ALF it improves transplant-free survival **only in coma grade I–II** (52% vs 30%); no benefit in grade III–IV and no overall survival benefit (Lee 2009). Paediatric non-paracetamol ALF: no benefit (worse under 2 years; Squires 2013).
b Hypertonic saline to **Na 145–155** (not 155–160); mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg if ICP rises.
c Early **CRRT** to clear ammonia; intubate grade III–IV for airway protection.
d **No** — only for bleeding or procedures (INR is a prognostic marker).

HY6|GIN-12.src: Lee WM et al., Gastroenterology 2009;137:856; Squires RH et al., Hepatology 2013;57:1542

fields.a:
a **1–3 mg IV bolus** (by severity), **doubling every 5 minutes** until atropinised (Eddleston, Lancet 2008).
b **Clear chest** (no wheeze or secretions), heart rate >80, systolic BP >80, **dry axillae**, pupils no longer pinpoint.
c Infusion of 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.
d Stop, then restart at **70–80% of the previous rate**.
e **Nicotinic** effects: weakness and paralysis.

**TOXIN** | **ANTIDOTE**
**Paracetamol** | **N-acetylcysteine**
**Opioids** | **Naloxone** 0.04–2 mg
**Organophosphate** | **Atropine** + **pralidoxime** 1–2 g over 30 min
**Methanol, ethylene glycol** | **Fomepizole** 15 mg/kg over 30 min; 10 mg/kg 12-hourly ×4; then 15 mg/kg 12-hourly
**Carbon monoxide** | **100% oxygen**; hyperbaric in some
**Cyanide** | **Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV** (70 mg/kg) over 15 min, repeat once if needed; sodium thiosulphate as adjunct. Sodium nitrite 300 mg IV is the older kit: avoid in smoke inhalation (adds methaemoglobin to COHb) and hypotension
**Methaemoglobinaemia** | **Methylene blue** 1–2 mg/kg
**Iron** | **Deferoxamine**, up to 15 mg/kg/h
fields.watch:
**WATCH**
Cyanide: hydroxocobalamin is first choice, especially in fire victims; nitrite would worsen oxygen carriage on top of carbon monoxide.

TOX01|TOX-13.src: Borron SW et al., Ann Emerg Med 2007 (hydroxocobalamin in smoke inhalation); standard toxicology (Goldfrank 11e); ERC 2021 special circumstances

fields.a:
Range 0 to 24. Higher scores predict higher mortality: an initial or highest SOFA **above 11** (or a mean above 5) carries mortality **above 80%** (Ferreira, JAMA 2001). A SOFA that rises over the first 48 h means mortality of at least 50%, whatever the start. These bands come from the original SOFA, not SOFA-2.
**Sepsis-3**
Sepsis = suspected or documented infection PLUS an acute rise in SOFA of 2 or more points from baseline.
Septic shock = sepsis PLUS a vasopressor requirement to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above PLUS lactate above 2 mmol/L, both persisting after adequate fluid resuscitation.

SC-A|SC-A-09.src: Ranzani OT et al. JAMA 2025 (SOFA-2); Singer M et al. JAMA 2016;315:801 (Sepsis-3)

fields.a:
Map the same 3 situations to their NON-PARAMETRIC equivalent test.
**Situation** | **Non-parametric test**
Single group (paired) | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** (numbers) · McNemar's test (categories)
Two independent groups | **Mann-Whitney U** (numbers) · Chi-square test (χ²) (categories)
Three or more groups | **Kruskal-Wallis** (numbers) · Chi-square / chi-square for trend (categories)
- Non-parametric tests are used for QUALITATIVE data, or for
quantitative data that is NOT normally distributed.
fields.watch:
The non-parametric twins of the t-tests are Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired) and
Mann-Whitney U (unpaired). McNemar and chi-square are for CATEGORIES: McNemar
when the same subjects are measured twice, chi-square for independent groups.

BS01B|BS-15.src: Standard biostatistics (Altman, Practical Statistics for Medical Research; Park 27e)

fields.a:
- A **FOREST PLOT** (see BIOSTATS BS-41 for the full card on reading one).
- The diamond = the SUMMARY measure — the **weighted pooled estimate** of all the studies (bigger, more precise studies count more). Its centre is the pooled point estimate and its width is the 95% CI; if the diamond crosses the line of no effect, the pooled result is not significant.

EPI01C|EPI-33.src: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, ch. 10

fields.a:
- **p-value** = probability that a result occurred by chance, expressed as a decimal from 0 (lowest chance) to 1 (maximum chance).
- SE (not SD) is used when working with p-values / confidence intervals.
**SE range** | **Confidence Interval**
±1 SE | 68%
±2 SE | 95% (zone of normalcy)
±3 SE | 99.7%
(99% CI = ±2.58 SE; 95% CI = ±1.96 SE)

BS01A|BS-11.src: Standard biostatistics (normal distribution z-values; Altman; Park 27e)

fields.a:
| **Disease +** | **Disease −**
Exposed | a | b
Non-exposed | c | d
- **Odds Ratio** = ad / bc (a cross-product ratio) — can be calculated in ANY design (cohort, cross-sectional, RCT; logistic regression gives ORs), but it is the ONLY valid measure in CASE-CONTROL studies.
- **Relative Risk** = [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)] = incidence in exposed / incidence in non-exposed — needs incidence, so only COHORT studies or RCTs.

EPI01A|EPI-04.src: Standard epidemiology (Rothman, Modern Epidemiology; Szumilas, J Can Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2010)

Check the **absolute number** AND the **variability /**
**collapsibility of the IVC with inspiration**
 | **Diameter** | **Collapsibility**
**LESS likely fluid responsive** | **>2 cm** | **<50%**
**MORE LIKELY fluid responsive** | **<1 cm** | **>50%**
(Suggests only: IVC alone predicts modestly, worse in spontaneous breathing; confirm with PLR or VTI change.)

CVS05B|ECHO-20.src: Long E et al., Shock 2017;47:550 (IVC variation meta-analysis); Monnet X, Teboul JL, PLR reviews; SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

fields.watch:
MSS runs the OPPOSITE way to every other row - low is
normal and high is severe, because it measures mitral-septal
SEPARATION. Its normal (<10) also overlaps the mild band (7-12)
as printed in the source. MAPSE and TAPSE share the same severe
cut-off (<6) but different normals (≥11 vs ≥17). TAPSE <17 mm = RV systolic
dysfunction (ASE 2015); normal has no upper cap (mean about 24 mm).

CVS05B|ECHO-39.src: Lang RM et al., ASE/EACVI chamber quantification, J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2015;28:1

fields.a:
a 1400–1500 mmol/day; cleared by the **liver and kidneys**.
b In septic shock mostly **adrenergic (beta-2) aerobic glycolysis** (driven by the Na/K pump), PLUS **reduced clearance** by the liver; tissue hypoxia with anaerobic glycolysis is only one contributor (more so in low-flow shock).
c **2 mmol/L** (part of the septic shock definition).
d A falling lactate means reperfusion and is linked to lower mortality in every patient group, whatever the starting value; a persistent rise means poor outcome. Changes are slow, so measure every **1–2 hours**.
e Beta-2 stimulation (e.g. adrenaline, salbutamol).

HEMO05A|PERF-05.src: Levy B et al., Lancet 2005;365:871; Garcia-Alvarez M et al., Crit Care 2014;18:503; SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

fields.q:
**Perfusion markers: level of evidence and main drawback.**
a Which marker is backed by meta-analysis?
b Which three are backed by randomised trials?
c Give the main drawback of lactate, ScvO2, mottling, CRT and sublingual microscopy
fields.a:
**Marker** | **Evidence** | **Drawback**
**Lactate** | Meta-analysis | Blood sample and lab time; raised in non-shock states
**ScvO2** | RCT | Needs a central line; less useful under anaesthesia
**O2 challenge test** | RCT | Special monitor; intubated patients only
**CO2 gap** | Cohort | Needs a central line and blood sampling
**Mottling** | Cohort | Limited in burns, amputations, dark skin
**CRT** | **RCT** (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2019; ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 2025) | Inter-rater variability
**Sublingual microscopy** | Cohort | Special device; mainly educational
fields.watch:
Your notes graded CRT as cohort-level; it now rests on two RCTs. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
(2019): 28-day mortality 34.9% vs 43.4%, P = 0.06. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025):
win ratio 1.16 (1.02–1.33) on a composite, with no mortality difference.

HEMO05B|PERF-20.src: Hernandez G et al., JAMA 2019 (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK); ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Investigators, JAMA 2025;334:1988; SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

fields.a:
TRIAL | TESTED | VERDICT
**Rivers** | EGDT | Mortality ↓ (46.5 to 30.5%)
**ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe** | EGDT vs usual care | No difference
**CLOVERS** | Restrictive vs liberal fluid | No difference
**ANDROMEDA-SHOCK** | CRT vs lactate | Not significant (P 0.06)
**ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2** (2025) | CRT-targeted vs usual care | Win ratio 1.16 (less organ support); mortality no different (26.5 vs 26.6%)
**ADRENAL** | Hydrocortisone | No difference; faster reversal
**APROCCHSS** | Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone | Mortality ↓

**Subtype** | **Vasoactive** | **Rationale**
**Classic wet & cold** | **Norepinephrine** (first line); inotropic agent | **Low CI, high SVR**. Norepinephrine is preferred: in SOAP II's cardiogenic-shock subgroup dopamine gave more arrhythmias and higher mortality, so it is not an equal choice (2017 AHA table listed both). Add inotrope once stable and **after revascularisation**
**Euvolaemic cold & dry** | As above, plus **small fluid boluses** | **LVEDP may be low** and patients may tolerate fluid boluses
**Vasodilatory warm & wet or mixed** | Norepinephrine; haemodynamics-guided therapy | **This subtype has LOW SVR**
**RV shock** | Fluid boluses; norepinephrine, dopamine or vasopressin; inotropes; **inhaled pulmonary vasodilators** | Maintain preload, **lower RV afterload (PVR)**, treat bradycardia, maintain AV synchrony. **Vasopressin raises SVR with neutral effect on PVR**
**Normotensive shock** | **Inotropic agent** or vasopressor | **SBP >90 mmHg** with relatively high SVR → initial inotropic therapy may be appropriate

CVS03|CS-31.src: De Backer D et al., NEJM 2010;362:779 (SOAP II); van Diepen S et al., AHA Scientific Statement, Circulation 2017;136:e232

fields.a:
**2 mL x body weight (kg) x %TBSA, titrated to urine output.**
Current ATLS guidance favours starting at this lower volume - rising to 4
mL/kg/%TBSA for high-voltage electrical injury (target urine 75–100 mL/h until it clears) - and titrating the infusion
rate against measured urine output, rather than infusing the full classic 4
mL/kg volume regardless of response.
The change reflects concern about fluid creep: over-resuscitation with the
classic formula driving massive oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome
and worse respiratory outcomes.
Either version's calculated volume is only a starting estimate. The actual
infusion rate is adjusted hourly against the patient's urine output.

SC-B|SC-B-16.src: ABA ABLS Provider Manual 2018 (primary manual not openly accessible; matches 2026 burn-centre ABLS badge card and VUMC/Minnesota protocols). Note: some local protocols (UAB) use 3 mL

fields.a:
- **Permissive hypotension**: SBP **80–90** (MAP **50–60**), normal mentation, palpable pulses, until bleeding is controlled; follow lactate and ScvO₂.
- **Not in TBI or spinal cord injury**: keep **MAP 80 or more** if GCS 8 or less.
- **Restrict crystalloid**: big volumes worsen bleeding (dilution, clot disruption), oedema, hepatocellular injury.
- **Haemostatic resuscitation**: blood products first, **RBC:FFP:platelets about 1:1:1**.
Penetrating torso: restrictive policy (SBP 60–70) lowers bleeding and 28-day mortality.

SPECIAL05B|POLY-15.src: Rossaint R et al. European guideline on major bleeding and coagulopathy after trauma, 6th ed. Crit Care 2023;27:80, Rec 13

fields.a:
- a Cofactor for clotting, cardiac contractility and vascular tone; monitor every 10 units transfused; keep **ionised Ca in the normal range (about 1.1–1.3 mmol/L)**; >0.9 mmol/L is an outdated threshold.
- b **rFVIIa**: off-label; no outcome benefit; thrombosis; status unclear (notes); last resort only *(standard teaching, not in your notes)*.
- c NASCIS II: high-dose methylprednisolone within 8 h improved motor recovery; NASCIS III: 48 h better than 24 h if started 3–8 h. **Now not recommended** (CNS, CAEP): harms, no long-term benefit.
- d Vitamins A, C, E: less inflammation; vitamin C may protect the kidneys.
fields.watch: European trauma bleeding guideline (2023): keep ionised calcium in the normal range during massive transfusion.

SPECIAL05B|POLY-22.src: Rossaint R et al. European trauma bleeding guideline 6th ed. Crit Care 2023;27:80, Rec 31

fields.a:
Skin burn **underestimates** deep muscle damage.
**Rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria**: high CK, dipstick positive for myoglobin.
Fluid **4 mL/kg/%TBSA** over the first 24 h; target **urine 75–100 mL/h** in adults (about 1–1.5 mL/kg/h; children about 2 mL/kg/h) until the pigment clears (ABLS).
**Alkalinise urine** with isotonic bicarbonate; **monitor calcium**.
ECG monitoring for arrhythmias; check compartments → **fasciotomy**.

MISC05B|BURN-12.src: ABA ABLS Provider Manual 2018 (via burn-centre/state protocols)

fields.a:
**First 24–72 h**: **Gram-positive** skin flora (Staph, Strep).
**Beyond 72 h**: **Gram-negatives**: **Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter**, Enterobacterales.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics → **fungi** (including filamentous) and MDR organisms.
**Leucocytosis** early (24–48 h), then **leucopenia**; procalcitonin only supports a sepsis diagnosis, it cannot confirm one. SSC 2026: do not use PCT to decide whether to START antibiotics; use it with clinical review to decide when to STOP.
**Systemic prophylaxis**: fewer pneumonias and wound infections but more **MRSA and MDR**: role unclear.

MISC05B|BURN-18.src: Prescott HC et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026, Crit Care Med 2026 (doi:10.1097/CCM.0000000000007075); de Jong E et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016 (SAPS)

fields.a:
**Enzyme** | **Pathogens** | **Resists** | **Treatment**
**KPC** | Entero-
bacterales | Penicillins, cephalo-
sporins, carbapenems | **Meropenem-vaborbactam**, **ceftazidime-avibactam**, **imipenem-relebactam**; cefiderocol alternative
**MBL** (NDM, VIM, IMP) | P. aeruginosa, S. maltophilia, Entero-
bacterales | Penicillins, cephalo-
sporins, carbapenems | Enterobacterales: **aztreonam-avibactam** or **ceftazidime-avibactam + AZTREONAM**, or cefiderocol. **MBL P. aeruginosa: cefiderocol preferred**
**OXA-48** | Entero-
bacterales (mainly Klebsiella); not Acinetobacter (CRAB carries OXA-23/24/58) | Penicillins, cephalo-
sporins, carbapenems | Ceftazidime-avibactam (preferred); cefiderocol
fields.watch:
All three resist the same three drug classes - the treatments
are what differ. MBL is the only one needing ADDED aztreonam (or aztreonam-avibactam) - and only for Enterobacterales; for MBL Pseudomonas use cefiderocol.

CCM06|MDR-12.src: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance (Tamma et al., Clin Infect Dis 2026, doi:10.1093/cid/ciag481) (MBL-Pseudomonas exception)

fields.q:
**Per IDSA 2026 for CRE, give**
**the agents for:**
a KPC producers
b NDM / MBL
c OXA-48-like producers
d The fallback common to all three
branches
fields.a:
**Branch** | **Agents**
**KPC producers** | **Meropenem-vaborbactam, ceftazidime-avibactam or imipenem-relebactam** (all preferred; slight edge to meropenem-vaborbactam); cefiderocol alternative
**NDM / MBL** | **Aztreonam-avibactam** (slightly favoured) or **ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam**; or **cefiderocol**
**OXA-48-like** | **Ceftazidime-avibactam** preferred (not meropenem-vaborbactam or imipenem-relebactam); cefiderocol alternative
- Polymyxins are not a routine fallback in IDSA (colistin only for simple cystitis); tigecycline/eravacycline only for non-bloodstream, non-urinary infections

CCM06|MDR-15.src: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance (Tamma et al., Clin Infect Dis 2026, doi:10.1093/cid/ciag481)

fields.a:
- **Ampicillin-sulbactam (2:1)**: high-dose sulbactam
**saturates penicillin binding proteins (PBP) 1
and 3**
- High dose = **27 g/day** (9 g of sulbactam), **infused
over 4 hours**
- Use combination therapy with **at least two agents**
- **Minocycline: 200 mg twice daily**, IV or oral
- **Polymyxin B**: never alone; only as a **partner** in combination, mild or severe CRAB
- **Cefiderocol**: a combination partner (with sulbactam-based therapy), not monotherapy
- First choice overall: **sulbactam-durlobactam + imipenem or meropenem** (IDSA 2026)

CCM06|MDR-22.src: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance (Tamma et al., Clin Infect Dis 2026, doi:10.1093/cid/ciag481)

fields.a:
- 1. **Meropenem-colistin combination is NOT
recommended**
- 2. **Sulbactam-durlobactam + imipenem or meropenem** is preferred (IDSA 2026). If unavailable, bridge with **high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam** (**9 g sulbactam/day** = 27 g/day, extended or continuous infusion) plus at least one other agent
- 3. Add an **additional agent** as combination
therapy: **minocycline, tigecycline, or polymyxin
B**
- 4. **Step down to oral therapy**
fields.watch:
High-dose sulbactam is now one number: 9 g of sulbactam a day (27 g/day of
ampicillin-sulbactam). The older 6-9 g range is outdated.

CCM06|MDR-23.src: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance (Tamma et al., Clin Infect Dis 2026, doi:10.1093/cid/ciag481)

fields.a:
IV **polymyxins** (colistin or polymyxin B) - strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence
Adjunctive **inhaled colistin** - weak recommendation, low-quality evidence
Inhaled colistin gives **faster clinical resolution** but **no mortality benefit**
**Now (IDSA 2026):** this is the 2016 IDSA/ATS position. Treat by organism with the newer agents (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol, sulbactam-durlobactam); polymyxins only as a last resort; nebulised colistin is not routine.

CCM03|VAP-29.src: Kalil AC et al., IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2016 (original source); IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance (Tamma et al., Clin Infect Dis 2026, doi:10.1093/cid/ciag481); Rello J et al., ESCMID/ESICM nebulised antibiotics position, Clin Microbiol Infect 2017

fields.q: **What are the elements of the VAP bundle (old IHI five, and SHEA 2022 now)?**
fields.a:
**Old IHI five:** head-of-bed elevation · oral care with chlorhexidine · stress ulcer prophylaxis · DVT prophylaxis · daily sedation hold + SBT

**SHEA 2022 (current) essential practices:**
- **Avoid intubation** where possible (HFNO/NIV)
- **Minimise sedation**; daily **SAT + SBT**
- **Early mobility**
- **Head of bed 30–45°**
- **Toothbrushing WITHOUT chlorhexidine** (chlorhexidine: possible mortality harm)
- **Early enteral feeding**

Add-on if rates stay high: subglottic secretion drainage. Stress ulcer and DVT prophylaxis are NOT VAP-prevention measures.

CCM03|VAP-32.src: Klompas M et al., SHEA/IDSA/APIC Compendium, Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol 2022;43:687

fields.a:
**Bezlotoxumab: monoclonal antibody against**
**TOXIN B**, FDA approved 2016. **Discontinued by Merck on 31 Jan 2025: no longer available**; for recurrence use fidaxomicin or a vancomycin taper/pulse, and FMT after 2 or more recurrences
For a **recurrent CDI episode within the last 6**
**months**, as a **co-intervention with**
**standard-of-care antibiotics**. Decreases
recurrence
**Dose 10 mg/kg IV**; half-life **18 days**; **1 injection**
**covers 3 months**
**Caution in patients with heart failure**
**FMT:** recommended for **recurrent** C. difficile
infection. Cure rate **70-90%**
Routes: oral capsule, NG tube, colonoscopy,
enema
**Not contraindicated in IBD or immunocompromised patients** (use with caution); avoid in neutropenia; risk of infection;
donor selection important

CCM11|CDI-24.src: Johnson S et al., IDSA/SHEA focused update, Clin Infect Dis 2021;73:e1029; Merck ZINPLAVA discontinuation announcement (Jan 2025)

fields.a:
- **Loading dose** for **aminoglycosides, β-lactams,**
**glycopeptides, tigecycline, colistin**: sized by Vd, **independent**
**of renal function**.
- **Maintenance**: by the eliminating organ (kidneys, liver).
- **Time-dependent**: bolus then **continuous or extended (4 h)**
**infusion**; best studied with pip-tazo and meropenem (also
vancomycin, ceftriaxone, cefepime); BLING III (2024) just missed significance (90-day
mortality 24.9% vs 26.8%), but the 2024 meta-analysis showed lower
mortality (RR 0.86); **SSC 2026: STRONG recommendation** for prolonged
β-lactam infusion after a loading dose.
- **Aminoglycosides**: large once-daily dose on **adjusted weight**.
- **TDM**: established for aminoglycosides and vancomycin; useful
for β-lactams in ARC.

SPECIAL04A|PK-11.src: Dulhunty JM et al., JAMA 2024;332:629 (BLING III); Abdul-Aziz MH et al., JAMA 2024;332:638; SSC 2026 (Prescott et al., Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med 2026)

fields.a:
**Infection** | **Agent**
**Yeast** (mucositis, BSI) | **Echinocandin first line** for candidaemia / suspected invasive candidiasis, especially in neutropenic or critically ill patients; **step down to fluconazole** once susceptible and stable. **C. krusei** and **C. glabrata** are fluconazole-resistant → stay on **echinocandins**
**Invasive mold** (aspergillosis m/c, zygomycosis, fusariosis) | **Voriconazole** or itraconazole; amphotericin B / liposomal formulation; echinocandins. Greatest risk: profound prolonged neutropenia, solid organ transplant, HSCT

D05C|IC-59.src: Pappas PG et al., IDSA candidiasis guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2016;62:e1; ECIL guidance

fields.a:
**Line** | **Agent**
**Primary** | **Voriconazole** (IV or oral) for most patients
Alternative primary | **Isavuconazole** (SECURE 2016) or **posaconazole** (non-inferior to voriconazole, 2021); **L-AmB** (liposomal amphotericin B)
**Salvage** | Itraconazole, echinocandins (caspofungin or micafungin). Combination from different classes may be used
- Start antifungals **early** - while diagnostic evaluation
is still in progress if IA is strongly suspected
- Minimum duration **6 to 12 weeks**; continue until
radiographic abnormalities stabilise and signs of
active infection disappear
- **Prophylaxis with POSACONAZOLE** (voriconazole an alternative): HSCT recipients
with GVHD; acute myelogenous leukaemia;
myelodysplastic syndrome

**Encephalopathy:** ABC; **head end low, 30 degrees**; rule out alternative causes; **dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6-q8h**; anti-ammonia measures; PLEX/RRT; AED for seizures
**Dengue-related HLH: must fulfil 5 of 8 parameters**
Fever ≥ **38.5°C**; splenomegaly; **fasting triglycerides** ≥ **265 mg/dL** or fibrinogen <150 mg/dL; **ferritin** ≥ **500 µg/L**; low/absent NK cell activity; haemophagocytosis on marrow/node/CSF; cytopenias in ≥2 cell lines; **soluble IL-2 receptor (CD25)** ≥ **2400 U/mL**
**Vaccination: licensed vaccines exist.** **CYD-TDV (Dengvaxia)**: licensed 2015 (Mexico), FDA 2019, seropositive recipients only, low efficacy against DEN-2; Sanofi announced its discontinuation in 2024 (production ends 2026). **TAK-003 (Qdenga)**: licensed 2022, WHO-prequalified May 2024; WHO recommends 2 doses, 3 months apart, at ages 6–16 in high-transmission settings. Under trial: TetraVax-DV, TDENV PIV, DNA vaccines

fields.a:
Trial | Details
DECRA | Patients with **DIFFUSE** traumatic brain injury. Early bifrontal DC for ICP **>20 mmHg for 15 min**: mortality **similar (19% vs 18%)** but **worse function** (unfavourable GOS-E 70% vs 51%)
RESCUE-ICP | Hutchinson et al. Medical care vs DC in **408** patients aged **10-65** with TBI (**not focal-only: about 80% diffuse**) and refractory raised ICP (**>25 mmHg**), last-tier DC. Outcome: GOS-E at 6 months
fields.why:
- RESCUE-ICP at 6 months: DC had **lower**
**mortality** (26.9% vs 48.9%), but **higher rates of vegetative state** (8.5% vs 2.1%),
lower severe disability and upper severe disability
fields.watch:
The two trials reached opposite-looking conclusions
because the QUESTIONS differ - DECRA did DC EARLY at a lower threshold (ICP >20
for 15 min), RESCUE-ICP used it as a LAST TIER for refractory ICP >25. Both
largely diffuse injury. DC trades mortality for disability.

fields.a:
Trial | Details
Eurotherm | Andrews PJD et al. (NEJM 2015). Hypothermia (**32-35°C**) + standard care vs standard care alone, in adults with intractably raised ICP (**>20 mmHg**). Primary outcome GOS-E at 6 months. **Stopped early for harm: worse functional outcome** (adjusted OR 1.53), trend to higher mortality
POLAR | **500** patients, 2 groups: normothermic vs early prophylactic hypothermia (**33°C**). **No change in outcomes**

Tier | Interventions
Standard measures | Head of bed elevation to **30°**; stool softeners; optimize venous drainage (head in midline)
Tier 1 | Transient hyperventilation (target ETCO2 **30 mmHg**); CSF drainage; sedation and analgesia
Tier 2 | **Hypertonic saline** infusion; **mannitol**
Tier 3 | Neuromuscular blockade; **pentobarbital-induced coma**; hypothermia; laparotomy
Branches: head CT → decompressive craniectomy; or additional neuromonitoring → revise ICP/CPP goals

This is the ENLS-style ladder (brief <2 h hyperventilation to PaCO2 30–35 in Tier 1). **SIBICC 2019 (TBI) differs:** Tier 1 keeps PaCO2 **35–38** and uses mannitol/HTS boluses and CSF drainage; mild hypocapnia **32–35** and paralysis are **Tier 2**; barbiturates, DC and hypothermia 35–36 are **Tier 3**.

fields.a:
**RSBI below 105 → SBT 30–120 min → extubate**
a **RSBI** = RR ÷ VT (L), measured over 1 min of **unassisted** breathing (T-piece, no PS/PEEP: support lowers it and inflates success); below ~100–105 predicts success (high sensitivity).
b **SBT 30–120 min** (PS 5–8 or T-piece) once a day; failed → full support for 24 h.
c **IMV** — longest weaning, most fatigue.
d Reduce PS by **3–6 cmH2O** steps, watching RR.
e **Prophylactic NIV** after extubation (fewer reintubations, ↓ mortality).

triggering). Higher with sepsis, fever, a narrow tube. Less accurate in COPD.

advises against incremental-PEEP RMs. Newer ARDS guidelines are stricter:

mediators → multi-organ failure.

fields.q:
**For the practical conduct of TTM, give:**
a The phases and their durations
b The nature of the rewarming phase
c What TTM involves, in three parts
d The stated preference
fields.a:
- **AHA 2025:** if not following commands, deliberate temperature control at **32–37.5 °C** (COR 1) for **at least 36 h** (COR 2a); **controlled rewarming no faster than 0.5 °C/h** (COR 2b)
- **ERC-ESICM 2025:** prevent fever (**>37.5 °C**) for at least **72 h**
- There is no fixed 24 h + 24 h schedule
- TTM involves: **careful monitoring of temperature with an INVASIVE temperature probe** • **targeting a safe temperature** • **coordinated MULTIMODAL control of shivering**
- **It is always preferable to PREVENT fever and shivering, if possible**
fields.watch: Rewarming is CONTROLLED (≤0.5 °C/h), not passive, and fever prevention runs on for 72 h - the intervention does not end when the target temperature is released.

fields.watch:
What DOES reduce mortality: low tidal volume and prone positioning.
The one drug exception is **early corticosteroids**: dexamethasone
lowered mortality in DEXA-ARDS (2020) and in COVID-19 (RECOVERY),
and early steroids are now conditionally recommended (ATS 2024,
SCCM 2024). No other drug has consistently reduced mortality.
Older grade tables (Harrison) still rate steroids D.
